description: We are VLDK, a team of students passionate about software development, space exploration, and game design. We're building an educational Moon/Mars colony simulator where players manage resources, protect astronauts, and solve realistic space survival challenges. Our skills include programming, backend development, AI, and system design. We welcome creative teammates interested in game development, pixel art, UI/UX, and space science!
summary:
ASTRA is a free browser game that turns kids aged 7–12 into the commanders of a small Mars base in Jezero Crater. There is nothing to install: players just open a link.

Players land at a half-built base and wake the builder robots. Then they keep their crew alive by balancing power, water, air, food and heat. They dig rooms underground to shield the crew from radiation, survive dust storms, and send radio messages that take minutes to reach Earth. Each machine has a short mini-game showing how the real thing works: wiping dust off solar panels, scrubbing CO₂ from the air, aiming an antenna at Earth.

Every fact comes from NASA missions such as Perseverance, Curiosity and InSight. Players collect 58 science cards in a Logbook, and every number in the game is labelled as a NASA measurement, an approximation or a game simplification. A mission report shows what the child learned.

Children in school today could be among the first people to live on Mars. ASTRA lets them try it first, so curiosity becomes real science through play.
details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRA is a free browser game for kids aged 7–12, set in Jezero Crater on Mars. A storyboard intro sets up a mystery: a rover went silent after hearing something strange, and builder robots were buried by a dust storm. The player lands, wakes the robots and grows an underground base, keeping the crew supplied with power, water, air, food and heat. Dust storms, broken machines and choices with real trade-offs keep things moving. Expeditions send a rover to sites around the crater, and radio messages arrive with a realistic Earth–Mars delay. Each machine has a short mini-game, nine in all, such as wiping dust off solar panels, balancing the CO₂ scrubber against the O₂ maker, or aiming a dish at Earth. A station AI called ASTRA guides the player in short, kid-friendly lines. At the end, a Mission Report awards up to 9 stars in three areas: Crew Care, Base Builder and Science Explorer.

Benefits

  • It teaches through doing: children learn why Martian soil protects against radiation by building rooms underground, not by reading about it.
  • 58 science cards, collected in a Logbook, link every game event to a real NASA finding.
  • Every number is labelled as a NASA measurement, an approximation or a game simplification, so the game never passes off fiction as fact.
  • It opens from a link with no install and no account, so it works on school laptops.

Intended impact

Today’s primary-school children may be the generation that first lives on Mars. We want them to feel that this future belongs to them, and to leave the game understanding the real problems explorers face (energy, air, water, radiation, distance) and how NASA missions study them.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: plain JavaScript (ES modules) with no frameworks or dependencies; HTML5 Canvas for rendering; Web Audio API for music and sound.
  • Testing: Node.js with its built-in test runner (500+ automated tests), and Playwright with headless Chrome for play-through checks.
  • Collaboration and hosting: Git and GitHub, a custom git sync tool, GitHub Actions for automated tests, GitHub Pages for hosting.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude to help with design documents, code review, bug fixes, testing and the trailer.
  • Data: NASA mission sources (Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight, MRO and others) are referenced in the code and the design document.

Creativity

  • Every game system is a real Mars problem in disguise: the soil the base is dug into is drawn from Perseverance’s radar layers, Curiosity’s mineral veins and an iron meteorite like “Cacao”.
  • The mini-games turn engineering into play a child can master in 15 seconds.
  • A mystery story keeps kids coming back, while the science stays honest.

Factors we considered

  • Age fit: short sentences, big buttons, sessions of a few minutes.
  • Emotional safety: no character ever dies, and mistakes lead to recovery, not punishment.
  • Accuracy: every fact is sourced and labelled.
  • Accessibility: volume controls, Reduce motion, Large text, screen-reader labels.
  • Reach: runs in any modern browser, all text kept ready for translation.
  • Privacy: no accounts, progress is saved only on the player’s own device.
